full_judgment:
7. Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed contended that when the Tribunal re-examined and recounted the ballot papers in presence of the parties and held some of them invalid, then the Tribunal's finding is a finding of facts which can hardly be disturbed in a writ-petition. He further contended that the Tribunal is not even required to give reasons for rejection of such ballot papers. In support of this contention he referred to two recent decisions of the Appellate Division reported in 27 D.L.R. at pages 117 and 118 respectively. We have perused these decisions. The numbers of invalid ballot papers involved in those two cases were very small- 5 (five) in one and 11(eleven) in another, whereas, the position in the present case is altogether different. These decisions of the Appellate Division cannot be interpreted to hold that the ballot papers found valid by the Presiding Officers in presence of the parties can be arbitrarily rejected by the Tribunal. In "Akbar Ali Vs. Raziur Rahman," 18 DLR (SC), 426, the Supreme Court confirmed a judgment of the High Court which interfered with a finding of an Election Tribunal on the ground of "wanton rejection of ballot papers". The number of ballot papers found wantonly rejected in that case was only six and those six ballot papers being the determining factor in the election result, the High Court called for them in order to see whether they were "spoilt" as found by the Tribunal, or "clean" as claimed by the petitioner. The High Court having held these votes valid set aside the Tribunal's order and directed that the petitioner be declared elected, In appeal before the Supreme Court it was contended that the High Court had assumed the role of an Appellate Court and substituted its finding for that of the Tribunal. The contention was rejected by the Supreme Court which observed that "it was not a case in which the High Court has substituted its own finding in place of the finding of the Tribunal". In view of the peculiar circumstances of the instant case; we called for the ballot papers and all other election materials. 

 8. On opening the packets of ballot papers we found out the 459 ballot papers of the petitioner which were declared invalid by the Tribunal. Class-wise, 21 ballot papers had no official seals thereon, 295 ballot papers had double marks and 143 ballot papers were shown as "illegible" or having marks made with substances other than rubber stamps. Of the 295 ballot papers having double marks, 245 were marked for the symbols "Hurricane" (of the petitioner) and "Balance" (of Respdt. No. 4); 45 ballot papers were marked for "Hurricane" and "Bicycle" (of Respdt. No.3); 3 ballot papers were marked for "Hurricane" on one hand and "Ink-pot", "Date-tree" and "Clock' on the other, It may be mentioned here that in respect of Symbols, Ink-pot and Cheek, there was no contesting candidate and accordingly to rules these two ballot papers would go to Hurricane; but this is not an important point. These 295 ballot papers having "double marks" are found to be in different ink and of different shapes, clearly indicating that these marks were not made at one time and place they bore official seals and as such were presumably handed over to voters. A voter who intended to vote for the "Hurricane" would not have marked the other symbol such as Balance or Bicycle unless, of course, he was totally ignorant about the procedure of voting. If he had marked both the places, the marks would have been of same size and ink. Different ink and size of the marks clearly indicate that these were made at different places out of motive which was not certainly good. 

 9. As to the 143 ballot papers found "illegible", it appears that the marks are well within the space of the Symbol "Hurricane" showing without any ambiguity that these ballot papers were marked for the petitioner. But the Election Rule, 40(3) requites that the marks should be made only with a rubber stamp. The Tribunal observed that some of the marks were made with hard substances. What we find is that it is not a case of "illegible marks" or "marks by any hard substance", but a case of deliberately defacing, blurring, mutilating and disfiguring the original marks in various crude ways, such as, by repeatedly pressing a rubber stamp or any other substance on the original marks and in some cases by putting thumb impressions thereon. In spite of this violence the original marks are discernible hi some cases. The purpose behind this was just to tamper with the ballot papers so that they could not be counted in favour of the candidate for whom they were intended. Of these 143 ballot papers, about 30 were found "indistinct" by the Tribunal. Marks may be indistinct if the rubber stamp is not adequately soaked with ink in the pad. Indistinct markings are found in some of the valid ballot papers as well. The ballot papers "illegible" and with "double marks" are found to have been tampered with from sinister motives. Ballot papers of this condition stand rejected under rules and the determination of their validity is a mere formality. As to 127 ballot papers of Respondent No. 2 which were held invalid by the Tribunal, most of them bore double marks like that of the petitioner. These ballot papers were, also tampered with, not for harming Respondent No. 2, but for putting up a "show". For, deduction of 127 ballot papers of Respondent No. 2 as against 459 ballot papers of the petitioner does not affect his interest in any way. As to 21 ballot papers having no office-seal, they are invalid according to rules. Inclusion thereof in the petitioners total might have been due to oversight as 23 ballot papers out of 127 of the Respondent No. 2 also had no office-seal but were nevertheless held valid by the Presiding Officers. 

 14. At the last stage of the hearing before us, the learned Attorney-General appeared in private capacity for Respdt. No. 2. He supported the contention of Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and limited himself to the question of powers of this Court in Writ jurisdiction as to "Certiorari". He has contended that the finding of facts arrived at by the Tribunal on re-examination of ballot papers in presence of the parties can hardly be interfered with under Article 102 of the Constitution. Firstly we do not think that determination of validity elf ballot papers is a question of facts; it is a mixed, question of law and facts. As to our jurisdiction under Article 102, we need not have been reminded that writ is a writ and not an appeal. Ordinarily, this Court does not interfere with the findings of a Sub-ordinate Court if the findings are arrived at on due consideration of relevant facts and correct appreciation of evidence being free from any unfairness of mired. If the findings are not so arrived at this Court has got every power to interfere therewith. In the case of Jamal Shah, reported in 18 D.L.R. (S.C.) the Supreme Court held that the High Court got jurisdiction under Article 98 of the late Constitution to interfere with the finding of an Election Tribunal. It was held by the Shifted Court:
